sm: The hosts open by teasing that the new Daily Wire film Confession is a documentary peering into our future, then turn to Ben Shapiro, who wrote it. He says the film is a big step for the company, directed by Vassal Marjo, a Venice Golden Lion nominee, with a cast holding seven Oscar nominations plus Rob Lowe. Shapiro argues it may be the first Daily Wire project that puts film first rather than conservative messaging first, while still resting on Christianity and anti-communism. One host confesses he expected to dislike it but was engrossed, especially from the second act through the climax.

Hosts say a film should make you feel an argument rather than just state it, and one says he was relieved because earlier conservative films resembled faith-based films that do their job but are hard to watch. Shapiro explains that he wrote the script and distrusts vanity projects, so he sent it to a well-known actor, who later had to drop out. Rob Lowe read it, was moved to tears, and begged to play the broken Russian literature professor and informer, even offering to shave his head. Shapiro adds that the director, James Franco, Nick Nolte, Brad Dourif, Emile Hirsch and Richard Brake all joined, and praises each performance.

Shapiro says the film was built around characters rather than arguments, so every piece has a reason and the ending feels inevitable. The shooting script ran only 82 pages, and he began with constraints, setting nearly everything in two rooms like an old studio-system picture. He names his influences as Arthur Koestler's Darkness at Noon, Timothy Snyder's Bloodlands, Life and Fate, and above all Dostoevsky's Grand Inquisitor argument. Another host says Christian films often fear giving the protagonist a real flaw, and the opening shot of Lowe licking vodka off the floor avoids that. Shapiro hopes the film is a gateway to great literature.

Asked why resurrect this story now, Shapiro says it was not a reaction to any one politician. He had been reading history and kept spotting echoes of earlier eras. He recalls that the company board had to approve the script and wondered about the audience, and his elevator pitch was that it is the most anti-communist, pro-Christian film ever made. A host calls it the strongest defense of Christianity since The Passion of the Christ. Hosts argue that communism's deepest problem is not economics but that it hates God, and that many Christian films ignore that following Christ costs something.

Shapiro agrees that sacrifice is central to religion and describes the final confrontation, where Franco takes the Grand Inquisitor's side and asks Lowe to sacrifice everything. He recalls the moment he realized the main character would have to atone to the other prisoner, since redemption requires actually repenting. The hosts discuss the ending, where the hero confesses both his crime against the state and his faith. They note the kiss on the forehead, the adopted-son theme, and a signal to read the end of the Grand Inquisitor. Shapiro adds that the film was shot on 35 millimeter in two-minute segments to keep the actors' intensity high.

The hosts praise the director's moving camera, which keeps a story set in drab dungeon rooms from feeling static. They note the film has no score except at the very beginning and end, and compare it to No Country for Old Men, saying a previous Daily Wire film that tried this did not work. They discuss the standing cell scene, which the director added because he grew up under communism and knew such cells existed at the Lubyanka. One host felt claustrophobic watching it, and another says it made him invest in the character. They also point to unscripted cutaways of Franco reacting while Lowe talks to his son.

Shapiro describes how the film was a collaborative process, with actors and director adding touches such as swirling a glass of vodka. He explains that he persuaded the director to have Franco ask Lowe to kneel with the word please, because a polite request is more frightening than an order. The hosts discuss how closely the film follows history. Shapiro says the set was built from scratch on an LA soundstage using photographs of the Lubyanka, and some details like the man mopping the floor are accurate, though layouts were changed for drama. A host asks whether political opponents would put conservatives against the wall, and they cite the reaction to Charlie Kirk's death.

The hosts watch a streamer's reaction to the trailer, mocking his dismissal of it as AI slop and noting the Chinese flag behind him. They discuss an article claiming Shapiro cannot be allowed to become a major Hollywood player. Shapiro says the left usually ignores conservative work, but cannot ignore a film with real actors and artistic credibility, and the outrage over the trailer showed they felt threatened. He says the company wants to hire the best people regardless of politics, and describes a casting rule of asking whether a Louisiana cousin would know the actor. They end on the surprise of seeing Nick Nolte and Franco on screen.

The hosts read praise for the film from Glenn Beck, David Limbaugh, Rod Dreher and others. Dreher called it one of the most philosophically and theologically profound and deeply Christian films he has seen, noting it was written by an Orthodox Jew. A host notes that critics such as Tucker Carlson and Candace Owens have not reviewed it. Shapiro then reveals that the mystery brunch companion Owens offered a ten thousand dollar reward to identify was actually Rob Lowe, and jokes he will give the money to Charlie Kirk's widow. Asked to make a closing pitch, the hosts say the film is relevant, historically accurate, moving, and unavailable elsewhere. Shapiro contrasts it with the provocative Run Hide Fight and Infidels, saying that Confession drew angrier reactions precisely because it plays in the left's sandbox with real artistic credibility. A final host calls it spiritually edifying and says it reminds Christians of the cost of their faith.
